overview.text: Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island or Isla de Pascua, is a Chilean island in the southeastern Pacific, about 3,700 kilometres from continental Chile. Its isolation and volcanic landscape form the setting for the distinctive culture of its Polynesian-origin people. From roughly the 11th to 17th centuries, Rapa Nui communities built ahu—ceremonial platforms—and carved monumental moai, which UNESCO describes as representing ancestors. Many statues were carved from volcanic tuff at Rano Raraku; unfinished figures there provide evidence of the carving process. The island’s archaeological landscape also includes rock art, caves and the ceremonial village of Orongo, making it significant for both its cultural heritage and archaeological record.

key_facts.text: Rapa Nui is the Indigenous name for Easter Island; Isla de Pascua is its Spanish name. It is Chilean territory in the Pacific, roughly 3,700 kilometres from continental Chile.
UNESCO describes the island’s early settlers as coming from Eastern Polynesia; their society built monumental works including moai and ahu.
Moai are large carved statues, generally made from yellow-brown volcanic tuff; UNESCO describes them as representing ancestors.
Ahu are ceremonial platforms. Ahu Tongariki is the largest and has 15 moai, according to UNESCO.
Rano Raraku was a moai quarry. Unfinished statues there help show how the figures were carved.
Rapa Nui National Park was inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 1995.
